::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
## Disclaimer

This lesson is for **education only**. The genotypes and patients used here are
fictional. Real prescribing decisions must follow the current version of the
guidelines, the approved drug label, and the judgement of the clinical team.
:::

## Overview {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note}
## Questions this lesson answers

- What is pharmacogenomics, and why does it matter for a pharmacist?
- What are ClinPGx, PharmGKB, CPIC and PharmCAT, and how do they relate?
- What do *star allele*, *diplotype*, *allele function* and *metabolizer phenotype* mean?
- How do you go from a patient's genotype to a prescribing recommendation?
- How do you judge how strong a recommendation, a drug label or a piece of evidence is?
- How do co-medications change the picture?
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this session you should be able to:

1. Explain the chain *genotype → diplotype → phenotype → recommendation*.
2. Find the CPIC guideline, drug labels and summary annotations for a gene-drug pair in ClinPGx.
3. Apply them to a patient case, including co-medications.
:::

|---|---|

| **Level** | Introductory |
| **Prerequisites** | Previous classes on Ensembl, UniProt, PDB and DrugBank |
| **Software needed** | A web browser only |

ClinPGx is recent (launched in July 2025) and is still integrating content from
CPIC. Tab names, menu labels and counts may differ slightly from what is
written here. If something is not where the text says, look around: the
information is almost certainly still there, just reorganised.

Ask yourself: what does it mean, for a clinical resource, that a guideline is
"updatable"?
:::

## Why is ClinPGx relevant for pharmaceutical sciences? {#sec-intro}

Two patients receive the same drug at the same dose. One responds well, the
other has no benefit, and a third may have a serious adverse reaction. Part of
this variability is **genetic**. **Pharmacogenomics (PGx)** studies how
inherited variation in our genes changes the way we respond to medicines.

In previous classes you followed one entity at a time: a **gene** in Ensembl, a
**protein** in UniProt, a **structure** in PDB, a **drug** in DrugBank.
ClinPGx sits on top of all of them and answers a clinical question:

> *"Given this patient's genotype, should I change the drug or the dose?"*

That is a question pharmacists will increasingly be asked to answer, which is
why this is our final database.

## About ClinPGx {#sec-about}

[ClinPGx](https://www.clinpgx.org/) is a free resource, managed at Stanford
University, that brings three projects under one roof:

| Project | What it is | What you get from it |
|---|---|---|
| **PharmGKB** | The Pharmacogenomics Knowledgebase, curating PGx literature since 2000 | Annotations of papers, drug labels and pathways |
| **CPIC** | The Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium | Peer-reviewed prescribing guidelines |
| **PharmCAT** | The Pharmacogenomics Clinical Annotation Tool | Software that turns a sequencing file (VCF) into a PGx report |

: The three components of ClinPGx {.striped tbl-colwidths="[18,42,40]"}

PharmGKB was renamed ClinPGx in July 2025, and old `pharmgkb.org` links now
redirect to the new site. In older papers you will still see the name
*PharmGKB*: it is the same knowledgebase. One renaming to remember: what
PharmGKB called **clinical annotations** are now called **summary
annotations**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

- Levels of evidence scoring: Whirl-Carrillo M *et al.*, *Clin Pharmacol Ther* 2021;110(3):563-572.
  <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8457105>
:::

## Key concepts before we start {#sec-concepts}

You only need six ideas to use ClinPGx well. Read them now; you will use each
one during the session.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📘 Concept 1: Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic genes

- **Pharmacokinetic (PK) genes** change *what the body does to the drug*:
  absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion. Most are enzymes (e.g. the
  cytochromes P450, **CYP2C19**, **CYP2D6**) or transporters (e.g. *SLCO1B1*).
- **Pharmacodynamic (PD) genes** change *what the drug does to the body*: the
  target (e.g. *VKORC1* for warfarin) or the immune response (e.g. *HLA-B* and
  severe skin reactions).
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📘 Concept 2: Star alleles and haplotypes

A gene can carry several variants at once. The combination of variants found
together on **one copy of a chromosome** is a **haplotype**. In pharmacogenes,
haplotypes are named with **star (\*) alleles**: `CYP2C19*1`, `CYP2C19*2`,
`CYP2C19*17`, and so on.

- `*1` is usually the reference (normal) allele.
- Each other star allele is defined by one or more **core variants**, often
  identified by their dbSNP **rsID** (e.g. `rs4244285`).
- The official naming authority for star alleles is
  [PharmVar](https://www.pharmvar.org/gene/CYP2C19).
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📘 Concept 3: Diplotype

We have **two** copies of each autosomal gene (one from each parent). The pair
of star alleles a person carries is their **diplotype**, written
`CYP2C19*1/*2`. A diplotype is the PGx equivalent of a genotype.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📘 Concept 4: Allele function and phenotype

Each star allele is assigned a **function**: *normal*, *decreased*, *no
function*, or *increased* function. Combining the two alleles of a diplotype
predicts a **phenotype**. For drug-metabolising enzymes the phenotypes are:

| Phenotype | Abbreviation | Enzyme activity |
|---|---|---|
| Ultrarapid metabolizer | UM | Much higher than normal |
| Rapid metabolizer | RM | Higher than normal |
| Normal metabolizer | NM | Normal |
| Intermediate metabolizer | IM | Reduced |
| Poor metabolizer | PM | Little or none |

: Standard metabolizer phenotypes {.striped}

**How do two alleles give one phenotype?** Think of each allele as
contributing some enzyme activity, and add the two contributions together.
For CYP2C19, the rules used by CPIC are:

| Allele 1 | Allele 2 | Phenotype |
|---|---|---|
| increased | increased | Ultrarapid (UM) |
| normal | increased | Rapid (RM) |
| normal | normal | Normal (NM) |
| normal *or* increased | no function | Intermediate (IM) |
| no function | no function | Poor (PM) |

: CYP2C19: from allele functions to phenotype (simplified from CPIC) {.striped}

Notice the last two rows: **one** no function allele is enough to reduce
activity, even when the other allele has increased function. These rules are
gene-specific, which is why each CPIC guideline has its own
genotype-to-phenotype table.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📘 Concept 5: Prodrugs turn the logic upside down

For most drugs, a **poor metabolizer** clears the drug slowly, so drug levels
rise and the risk of **toxicity** increases. But a **prodrug** is inactive
until an enzyme converts it into the active form. For a prodrug, a poor
metabolizer makes *less* active drug, so the risk is **lack of efficacy**.

Clopidogrel, our example today, is a prodrug activated mainly by CYP2C19.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📘 Concept 6: The ClinPGx knowledge pyramid

ClinPGx builds knowledge in layers, from raw literature to clinical action:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "From published papers to prescribing guidance."
flowchart BT
  A["Published papers<br/>(PubMed)"] --> B["Variant annotations<br/>one finding from one paper"]
  B --> C["Summary annotations<br/>all findings for one variant-drug pair,<br/>graded with a level of evidence"]
  C --> D["Guidelines and drug labels<br/>CPIC, DPWG, FDA, EMA...<br/>what to do in the clinic"]
```

The higher you go, the more curated and the more clinically actionable the
information becomes.
:::

The whole lesson follows this chain:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "The pharmacogenomic reasoning chain used in this lesson."
flowchart LR
  G["Genotype<br/>rs4244285 G/A"] --> D["Diplotype<br/>CYP2C19*1/*2"]
  D --> P["Phenotype<br/>Intermediate metabolizer"]
  P --> R["Recommendation<br/>CPIC guideline"]
```

2. Without clicking yet, scroll the homepage and note its main sections.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. Which kinds of entities can you search for?
2. Open the **gene-drug pairs** list (<https://www.clinpgx.org/pairs>). What is it built from?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. Genes, drugs (called *chemicals*), variants and haplotypes, diseases, as well as guidelines, labels, pathways and literature.
2. It lists gene-drug pairs that have been annotated in guidelines or drug labels from **CPIC**, **DPWG** (the Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group) and the **FDA**. It is a quick way to see which pairs are clinically relevant.
:::
::::

## The gene page: CYP2C19 {#sec-gene}

As in UniProt, the best way to find an entry is a **unique identifier**, here
the official HGNC gene symbol.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: open the CYP2C19 page

1. Type `CYP2C19` in the search bar.
2. Select the **gene** result (not a drug or a variant).
3. Note the identifier in the URL. It starts with `PA` (e.g. `PA124`).
4. Browse the tabs of the gene page.
:::

Every ClinPGx object has a stable **PA identifier** (a legacy of PharmGKB), in
the same way that UniProt has accessions like `P04000` and DrugBank has
identifiers like `DB00758`.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. CYP2C19 is labelled a **VIP**. What does that mean?
2. List three drugs (or drug classes) that have a CPIC guideline for CYP2C19.
3. In the cross-references, find the identifiers for **Ensembl** and **UniProt**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. *Very Important Pharmacogene*: a gene with strong, well documented pharmacogenomic relevance, for which ClinPGx curators write a dedicated summary.
2. Among others: clopidogrel, proton pump inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole, pantoprazole), voriconazole, and several antidepressants (e.g. citalopram, sertraline). Keep omeprazole in mind: it comes back in the patient case.
3. Ensembl `ENSG00000165841` (chromosome 10) and UniProt `P33261` (CP2CJ_HUMAN).
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔗 Connection: UniProt and PDB

The UniProt entry [P33261](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P33261/entry) and
the PDB structure [4GQS](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/4GQS) describe the
*protein*: a heme-containing enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells.
ClinPGx adds the clinical layer: *what happens to patients* when its gene varies.
:::

## From alleles to phenotype {#sec-alleles}

CPIC guidelines are written **per phenotype**, not per variant. So the single
most useful skill in ClinPGx is translating a genotype into a phenotype.

### Allele function {#sec-allele-function}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: the allele function table

1. Open the allele function pages: <https://www.clinpgx.org/alleleFunctions>.
2. Select **CYP2C19**.
3. Find the alleles `*1`, `*2`, `*3` and `*17`.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. What is the function assigned to `*1`, `*2`, `*3` and `*17`?
2. Each row of the table below is a patient, described by their two CYP2C19
   alleles (their diplotype). For each patient, work in two steps:
   a. write down the function of each of the two alleles (your answer to
      question 1);
   b. use the rules table at the end of **Concept 4** to find the phenotype
      that matches that pair of functions.

| Patient diplotype | Function of allele 1 + allele 2 | Phenotype |
|---|---|---|
| `*1/*1` | normal + normal | ? |
| `*1/*17` | ? | ? |
| `*17/*17` | ? | ? |
| `*2/*17` | ? | ? |
| `*2/*3` | ? | ? |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. `*1` normal function; `*2` and `*3` no function; `*17` increased function.
2. Phenotypes:

| Patient diplotype | Function of allele 1 + allele 2 | Phenotype |
|---|---|---|
| `*1/*1` | normal + normal | Normal metabolizer (NM) |
| `*1/*17` | normal + increased | Rapid metabolizer (RM) |
| `*17/*17` | increased + increased | Ultrarapid metabolizer (UM) |
| `*2/*17` | no function + increased | Intermediate metabolizer (IM) |
| `*2/*3` | no function + no function | Poor metabolizer (PM) |

: CYP2C19 diplotype to phenotype {.striped}

The tricky one is `*2/*17`: the increased function of `*17` does **not**
compensate for the loss of `*2`, so CPIC classifies it as intermediate.
:::
::::

### The variant behind CYP2C19\*2 {#sec-variant}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: one variant, two databases

1. In ClinPGx, search for `rs4244285` and open the **variant** page.
2. In a new tab, open the same variant in **Ensembl**:
   <https://www.ensembl.org/Homo_sapiens/Variation/Explore?v=rs4244285>.
3. In Ensembl, look at the predicted **consequence** of the variant on the
   transcript.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. Which star allele does `rs4244285` define?
2. What consequence does Ensembl predict for the protein sequence?
3. If the amino acid does not change, how can this be a *no function* allele?
   *(Hint: read the **Description** in the Overview section of the ClinPGx
   variant page.)*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. `CYP2C19*2` (c.681G>A).
2. Ensembl reports it as a **synonymous** variant (the codon still encodes proline 227).
3. The change creates an **aberrant splice site**. The mRNA is spliced incorrectly, the reading frame shifts, and a truncated, non-functional enzyme is produced. This is a classic lesson: *"synonymous" does not mean "harmless"*. Automatic predictors look at the codon; curated databases like ClinPGx integrate experimental evidence.
:::
::::

## The drug page: clopidogrel {#sec-drug}

The drug page is where most clinical questions start: it gathers, in one
place, the **guidelines** and **drug labels** for that drug (in the
*Prescribing Info* area) and the **summary annotations** from the literature.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: open the clopidogrel page

1. Search for `clopidogrel` and open the **chemical** page.
2. In the cross-references, find the **DrugBank** identifier.
3. Locate (do not read in detail yet) the **guidelines**, the **drug labels**
   and the **summary annotations**. You will use all three in the patient case.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. What is the DrugBank identifier for clopidogrel?
2. Why is CYP2C19 so important for this particular drug? *(Hint: Concept 5.)*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. `DB00758`. In [DrugBank](https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00758) you can see its target (the platelet P2Y12 receptor), its metabolising enzymes and its drug interactions.
2. Clopidogrel is a **prodrug**. CYP2C19 performs most of its conversion to the active metabolite. Patients with low CYP2C19 activity make less active drug, so their platelets are less inhibited and they have a higher risk of heart attack, stroke or stent thrombosis.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📘 Concept 7: three scales to judge what you find

Everything on the drug page comes with a grade. You will need these three
scales in the patient case, so keep this box open.

**1. CPIC level of the gene-drug pair** (shown in the gene-drug pairs list)

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | Genetic information **should** be used to change prescribing |
| **B** | Genetic information **could** be used to change prescribing |
| **C / D** | No prescribing action recommended |

Inside a guideline, each recommendation also has a **strength**: *strong*,
*moderate* or *optional*.

**2. Pharmacogenomic level of a drug label** (FDA, EMA, PMDA, ...)

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Testing required** | Genetic testing must be done before prescribing |
| **Testing recommended** | Testing is recommended |
| **Actionable PGx** | The label suggests a change based on genotype, without requiring testing |
| **Informative PGx** | The label mentions a gene-drug effect, with no clinical action |

**3. Level of evidence of a summary annotation** (one variant, one drug)

| Level | Evidence |
|---|---|
| **1A** | High: variant-specific guidance in a guideline or FDA label |
| **1B** | High: strong, replicated association, but no guidance yet |
| **2A / 2B** | Moderate |
| **3** | Low: single or conflicting studies |
| **4** | The evidence does not support an association |
:::

## The patient case {#sec-case}

This is the core of the lesson. You will use ClinPGx the way a hospital
pharmacist would: to answer a real prescribing question, step by step.

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## 🩺 The patient

**Mr. A.**, 62 years old, has just had a coronary stent implanted (PCI) after
an acute coronary syndrome. The cardiologist plans to prescribe **clopidogrel**
(with aspirin). He has no history of stroke or major bleeding.

He has been taking **omeprazole** 20 mg/day for more than a year for gastric
protection.

A pharmacogenomic test reports: **CYP2C19 `*1/*2`**.

You are asked to review his medication.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question 1: What is his phenotype?

Translate Mr. A.'s diplotype into a CYP2C19 phenotype.

*Where to look:* the allele function table and the rules in Concept 4 (see
@sec-allele-function).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
`*1` (normal function) + `*2` (no function) = **intermediate metabolizer (IM)**.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question 2: What does the guideline recommend?

What does CPIC recommend for a CYP2C19 intermediate metabolizer who needs
antiplatelet therapy after PCI? How strong is the recommendation? Would the
recommendation be different if he were a poor metabolizer?

*Where to look:* clopidogrel page → guidelines → **CPIC guideline for CYP2C19
and clopidogrel**. Select the cardiovascular indication (ACS/PCI) and the
phenotype.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Based on the 2022 CPIC update:

- **Intermediate metabolizer:** avoid standard-dose clopidogrel if possible;
  use **prasugrel or ticagrelor** at standard dose if there is no
  contraindication. Strength: **moderate**.
- **Poor metabolizer:** same advice, but the strength is **strong**.

Increasing the clopidogrel dose is not the solution: these patients cannot
make enough active metabolite. Prasugrel and ticagrelor do not depend on
CYP2C19 in the same way. Mr. A. has no history of stroke (a contraindication
for prasugrel), so both alternatives are possible.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question 3: How much can we trust this?

a. What is the **CPIC level** of the CYP2C19-clopidogrel pair?
b. What is the **level of evidence** of the summary annotation for `rs4244285`
   and clopidogrel?
c. Open that summary annotation and scroll to the supporting papers. Do they
   all agree?

*Where to look:* (a) the gene-drug pairs list <https://www.clinpgx.org/pairs>;
(b, c) the summary annotations on the clopidogrel page, filtered for
`rs4244285`. Use Concept 7 to interpret the grades.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
a. **Level A**: genetic information *should* be used to change prescribing.
b. **Level 1A**: the variant has specific guidance in a guideline and a drug
   label, and is supported by many independent studies.
c. No. Some studies find an association, others do not (different
   populations, sample sizes, outcomes). This is why ClinPGx summarises and
   grades many papers instead of relying on any single one, and partly why the
   recommendation for intermediate metabolizers is *moderate* rather than
   *strong*.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question 4: What do the regulators say?

a. Which agencies have a pharmacogenomic label annotation for clopidogrel?
b. Which PGx level does ClinPGx assign to the **FDA** label? Is testing required?
c. The FDA label has a **boxed warning**. What is it about?
d. Does the label say the same thing as CPIC about intermediate metabolizers?

*Where to look:* clopidogrel page → **drug labels**. Use Concept 7.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
a. Several, including the FDA, EMA, PMDA, Swissmedic and Health Canada (the
   exact list may vary).
b. **Actionable PGx** (at the time of writing). Testing is not required.
c. Diminished antiplatelet effect in patients who are CYP2C19 **poor**
   metabolizers; the label advises considering another P2Y12 inhibitor.
d. Not exactly. The FDA warning focuses on poor metabolizers, while CPIC also
   recommends alternatives for intermediate metabolizers. Labels and
   guidelines are written by different bodies, at different times, with
   different purposes. That is why ClinPGx shows both side by side.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question 5: What about his omeprazole?

Mr. A.'s genotype and his omeprazole interact in **two** ways.

a. Omeprazole is itself metabolised (inactivated) by CYP2C19. What does CPIC
   recommend for an intermediate metabolizer on **long-term** omeprazole?
b. Omeprazole also **inhibits** CYP2C19. What does that mean for his
   clopidogrel? What is this effect called?
c. Compare the effect of his genotype on clopidogrel and on omeprazole. Why
   does it go in opposite directions?

*Where to look:* (a) omeprazole page → **CPIC guideline for CYP2C19 and proton
pump inhibitors**; (b) the clopidogrel drug labels in ClinPGx, and the
clopidogrel-omeprazole interaction in
[DrugBank](https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00758).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
a. Start with the standard dose. For chronic therapy (more than 12 weeks) with
   symptoms controlled, **consider a 50% dose reduction** and monitor
   efficacy. Intermediate metabolizers clear omeprazole more slowly, so they
   have higher exposure, which increases the risk of long-term side effects
   (e.g. infections, fractures).
b. Omeprazole reduces CYP2C19 activity even further, so even less clopidogrel
   is activated. The FDA label advises **avoiding omeprazole and esomeprazole**
   with clopidogrel. This is **phenoconversion**: a co-administered drug
   makes the patient behave like a lower-activity phenotype than his genotype
   predicts (here, an intermediate metabolizer moving towards a poor
   metabolizer). Genes are not the whole story: always check the full
   medication list.
c. Clopidogrel is a **prodrug** (CYP2C19 activates it): lower activity means
   *less* effect. Omeprazole is an **active drug** (CYP2C19 inactivates it):
   lower activity means *more* exposure. Same enzyme, same patient, opposite
   consequences (Concept 5).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question 6: Your final recommendation

a. Open [PharmDOG](https://pharmdog.clinpgx.org/), the ClinPGx prescribing
   tool. Enter Mr. A.'s CYP2C19 result and his two drugs (clopidogrel and
   omeprazole). Does the output match your answers to Questions 2 and 5?
   Does it warn you about the omeprazole-clopidogrel interaction?
b. Write a short note (3 to 4 sentences) to the cardiologist with your
   recommendation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
a. PharmDOG should confirm the intermediate metabolizer phenotype and the
   CPIC recommendations for both drugs. At the time of writing, its
   phenoconversion feature covered CYP2D6 only, so it may **not** warn you
   that omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19. Tools help, but the pharmacist still has
   to check drug-drug interactions (e.g. in DrugBank).
b. Example note:

> *Mr. A. is a CYP2C19 intermediate metabolizer (`*1/*2`), so he is expected
> to activate clopidogrel poorly. According to the CPIC guideline (moderate
> recommendation), we suggest ticagrelor or prasugrel instead of clopidogrel,
> as he has no contraindication. This also avoids the clopidogrel-omeprazole
> interaction. Omeprazole can be continued; given his genotype and long-term
> use, a dose reduction could be considered if his symptoms remain controlled.*
:::
::::

## Key points {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Take home messages

- **ClinPGx** (formerly PharmGKB) integrates PharmGKB, CPIC and PharmCAT into one free pharmacogenomics resource.
- The core reasoning is **genotype → diplotype → phenotype → recommendation**.
- The **drug page** is the usual starting point: it gathers guidelines, drug labels and summary annotations.
- **CPIC guidelines** say *what to do*; **drug labels** give the regulatory position; **levels of evidence** say *how much to trust* an association.
- For **prodrugs** such as clopidogrel, low enzyme activity means *less* effect, not more toxicity.
- Genes are not the whole story: co-medications can cause **phenoconversion**.
- Stable identifiers connect ClinPGx to **Ensembl**, **UniProt**, **PDB** and **DrugBank**.
:::
